title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy
date_evidence: Allen, Jeffrey S. (2026). "Monitoring AI Adoption in the U.S. Economy," FEDS Notes. Washington: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, April 03, 2026
key_claim: Three high-quality US surveys give widely divergent AI-adoption estimates: about 18% of firms (Census BTOS), about 41% of workers (Real-Time Population Survey), and about 78% employment-weighted (Survey of Business Uncertainty).
frame_summary: There is no single AI adoption rate; the estimates diverge chiefly because of differences in unit of analysis, sampling, question framing and materiality, so the trend must be read through those drivers rather than a headline number.
verbatim_quote: The SBU estimates an employment-weighted firm AI adoption rate of around 78 percent and an LLM adoption rate of about 54 percent.
verbatim_list: The right panel of figure 2 shows that work-related GenAI adoption reported in the RPS stands at about 41 percent of the workforce, and non-work-related usage at about 50 percent of the population as of the latest survey in November 2025.
Adoption stood at about 18 percent of firms at the end of 2025.
Table 1 shows that there are notable differences in the estimated adoption rates among the three surveys.

The biggest driver of variation in these estimates likely relates to differences in sampling distributions and units of analysis, but question framing, the materiality of reported usage, information asymmetries between different target respondents, and social desirability bias may play a role as well.
notes: Structural anchor: canonical primary source for the measurement-divergence framing, 106 days before scan date (within 6 months). Quotes confirmed on the live page via WebFetch; provenance recorded manually because the sandbox has no network egress for the automated re-fetch.

title: AI Use at U.S. Businesses: Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users
key_claim: Under the Business Trends and Outlook Survey, overall US firm AI use ran between 17% and 20% from December 2025 to May 2026; 37% of firms with at least 250 employees reported using AI, and the survey question was broadened in November 2025 from AI in producing goods or services to AI in any business function.
frame_summary: Census presents AI use as growing across firm sizes and concentrated in large firms and knowledge sectors, having broadened its question to capture use across any business function.
verbatim_quote: For example, 37% of firms with at least 250 employees reported using AI in their business operations.
verbatim_list: The BTOS data (December 2025 to May 2026) show that overall AI usage hovered between 17% and 20% — and that between 20% and 23% of businesses expected to be using it in the next six months.

As of May 3, 2026, the AI use rates in the Information (39.7%) and Finance and Insurance (33.9%) sectors were both higher than the national rate (19.8%) but neither reported significant shifts since December.
In the data collection period ending May 3, 2026, 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees said they used AI.

Originally framed around AI use “in producing goods or services,” rather than to carry out simple tasks like drafting emails, the Census Bureau revised the wording last November to ask businesses whether they were using AI “in any business function.”
notes: Live-verified via WebFetch; publication date read from meta article:published_time. The broadened-question detail is the load-bearing measurement point.

publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER Working Paper 35141), mirroring US Census Bureau CES Working Paper CES-WP-26-25
title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
key_claim: In November 2025 to January 2026, 18% of US firms used AI in at least one business function (32% employment-weighted), but use is shallow: 57% of adopters use AI in three or fewer functions, and adoption reaches 50-60% only among very large knowledge-sector firms.
frame_summary: AI diffusion is broad but shallow and concentrated: present across many firms yet confined to a few functions and heaviest among large firms in information, professional services and finance.
verbatim_quote: During Nov 2025–Jan 2026, 18% of firms used AI in at least one function (32%, employment-weighted), with adoption expected to reach 22% within six months.
verbatim_list: 57% of users integrate AI in three or fewer business functions, most often Sales and Marketing, Strategy, and IT.

AI use is substantially higher in large firms and knowledge-intensive sectors, with use rates reaching 50%-60% (60%-70%, employment-weighted) for very large firms in the Information, Professional Services, and Finance sectors.
notes: NBER mirror used to keep the record inside the 90-day window (Census CES page carries a 15/04 published date, last revised 07/05). Figures cross-checked against both landing pages.

publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (On the Economy)
title: Measuring AI Adoption among Firms: How You Ask Matters
key_claim: US worker surveys put AI use at around 35% to 40% of workers while the main firm survey put business AI adoption at just 5% to 7%, a gap driven largely by how the survey question is framed rather than real behaviour.
frame_summary: The apparent adoption gap between workers and firms is mostly a measurement artefact of question design; broadening the Census question nearly doubled measured firm adoption.
verbatim_quote: Worker surveys suggest that somewhere around 35% to 40% of workers use AI on the job, while the main U.S. firm survey put AI adoption among businesses at just 5% to 7%.
notes: Directly on-thesis Tier 1 source that question framing drives the divergence. Live-verified via WebFetch.

title: Census: AI Adoption Accelerating Across U.S. Businesses, but Use Cases Remain Narrow
key_claim: Trade coverage of the new Census data reads AI adoption as spreading but concentrated among larger firms and a narrow set of operational functions rather than enterprise-wide transformation.
frame_summary: Firms have moved past experimentation but most remain in early, targeted deployment focused on a few practical use cases, not broad transformation.
verbatim_quote: New findings from the U.S. Census Bureau show AI adoption continuing to spread across American businesses, though usage remains heavily concentrated among larger firms and specific operational functions.
notes: Tier 3 corroboration of the breadth-without-depth reading, verified via WebFetch.

title: AI sticker shock hits corporate America
key_claim: Corporate leaders are questioning whether soaring AI spending delivers returns; a model-training executive tells Axios that in practice AI mostly works for coding, so broad deployment drives up IT bills without matching returns.
frame_summary: Enterprises are swinging back from indiscriminate AI use as costs outrun measurable returns, exposing a gap between spend and value.
verbatim_quote: While the market views these tools as  working equally well across the enterprise, Ansari says "the reality of AI right now is that it only works for coding."
verbatim_list: Corporate leaders are starting to question whether soaring AI spending is delivering meaningful returns.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism corroborating shallow material return; live-verified via WebFetch. Quote is Micro1 CEO Ali Ansari, reported by Axios.

title: The AI Value Levers: How Innovation-Focused Strategies Outperform, for Firms and Workers
key_claim: Firms that deploy AI toward innovation and growth generate stronger returns than those using it merely to cut labour costs, and real value is available where AI is genuinely integrated.
frame_summary: Counter to the broad-but-shallow reading: AI is materially valuable when integrated through growth-oriented levers, and firms under-exploit that depth by over-focusing on cost reduction.
verbatim_quote: Prior academic research, discussed below, has found that companies that apply technology like AI toward innovation tend to generate stronger returns than those that focus on cost reduction.
